summary: This document profiles the ACME Authority Token for phone-number certificates. It is meant for automatically and properly issuing certificates to Voice over IP providers that take part in Secure Telephone Identity (STI), using the TNAuthList field found in STI certificates. It is a narrow application of the generic mechanism in RFC 9447.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone companies need special badges that prove which phone numbers they may use. This document lets a computer hand out those badges automatically, after checking the company is allowed.

questions: how does acme work for phone numbers
subtitle: How a phone provider proves, through ACME, that it may get a certificate for particular telephone numbers.

tldr.problem: Secure Telephone Identity (STI) certificates list the telephone numbers or provider codes a caller may claim, but ACME had no way to check that a requester really has authority over those numbers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a TNAuthList identifier type to ACME and uses the Authority Token challenge from RFC 9447: a trusted Token Authority issues a signed token naming the TNAuthList, and the ACME server validates it before issuing the certificate.
tldr.outcome: Voice over IP providers can obtain STI certificates automatically and with authorization, to help detect impersonation of callers.

today: RFC 9448 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It builds on the generic Authority Token mechanism of RFC 9447.

sections.title: Why Phone Certificates Need Authority Proof
sections.content:
ACME (RFC 8555) automates certificate issuance, and RFC 9447 extends it so that a third party, a Token Authority, can vouch for a client's authority over a resource. This RFC is a profile of that Authority Token mechanism.

It targets the Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR) problem: the need for Internet credentials that attest authority for the originator of VoIP calls, in order to detect impersonation. The RFC calls impersonation an enabler of illegal robocalling, voicemail hacking and swatting. The credentials sign Personal Assertion Tokens (PASSporTs), which can be carried by protocols such as SIP.

The only credentials currently defined for this purpose are the certificates of RFC 8226 using the TNAuthList, which can hold a Service Provider Code (SPC), a telephone number, or sets of numbers or number blocks. The RFC also allows a telephone authority to authorize certificates that are themselves CAs, for delegation as defined in RFC 9060.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can say they own a phone number. This gives phone companies a way to show a trusted badge-giver's signature, so the badge office can check before handing out an official badge.

sections.title: The TNAuthList Identifier in a New Order
sections.content:
A normal ACME new-order request lists identifiers. This RFC defines a new identifier type, TNAuthList, whose value holds the details of the requested TNAuthList. The ASN.1 object MUST be DER encoded and then turned into a string with base64url, without padding characters.

The ACME server answers a valid order by creating an authorization object with a challenge, and the order is returned in a 201 (Created) response. IANA added TNAuthList to the "ACME Identifier Types" registry.
sections.plainLanguage: When a phone company asks for a badge, it writes the list of numbers it wants in a special packed-up code on the order form.

sections.title: The tkauth-01 Challenge
sections.content:
The ACME client fetches the authorization object and finds a challenge of type tkauth-01 with a tkauth-type of atc, as defined in RFC 9447. The CA uses it to verify that the client has authenticated and is authorized for the requested resources.

The challenge may include a token-authority URL. It is only used where the VoIP network requires the CA to identify the Token Authority, which the RFC says is currently not the case for the SHAKEN certificate framework governance. If it is present, the client MAY use it; if not, the client MUST identify the Token Authority from locally configured information or policy.

The client answers the challenge by posting the Authority Token in a new tkauth field of the challenge response.
sections.plainLanguage: The badge office hands the company a puzzle: go get a signed note from the trusted authority. The company fetches the note and hands it back.

sections.title: The TNAuthList Authority Token
sections.content:
The token is a JSON Web Token profile. Its payload MUST include the claims exp (expiry time), jti (unique identifier for the token transaction) and atc, and MAY include iss, a URL identifying the Token Authority.

The atc claim is a JSON object with these keys:

  • tktype: MUST be the string TNAuthList.
  • tkvalue: MUST be the base64url encoding of the DER-encoded TNAuthList extension.
  • ca: optional boolean, true if the certificate may be a CA certificate for delegation; false by default.
  • fingerprint: MUST be present, built from the ACME account key thumbprint as in RFC 8555 Section 8.1.

The fingerprint ties the token to the ACME account. The Token Authority does not verify it; it only signs it into the token so that the ACME server can check that the token came from the party that controls the ACME client.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed note says which numbers are allowed, when the note stops working, and carries a stamp that matches the company's own account so nobody else can reuse it.

sections.title: Getting the Token and Validating It
sections.content:
The client gets the token by an HTTP POST to the Token Authority, using an account identifier and some authorization credentials. The body is a JSON object with the requested claim values. A successful reply is 200 (OK) with a token key. If the credentials are invalid or the account does not exist, the response code MUST be 403 (Forbidden). Before issuing, the Token Authority MUST check that the TNAuthList accurately matches the SPC or telephone number resources the requester is authorized to represent.

The token may cover a subset of the client's authority. To limit what any CA can learn about a client's resources, the RFC says scopes should be limited to only the resources the requested certificate will attest where there is a privacy risk.

The ACME server then performs nine checks. These include that the atc claim is well formed, that x5u or x5c points to a trusted issuer of Authority Tokens, that the signature verifies, that tktype is TNAuthList, that tkvalue equals the identifier from the original order, that the token has not expired, that the fingerprint matches the account key, and that ca matches the CA boolean in the Basic Constraints extension of the CSR. If all pass, the challenge status MUST be valid; otherwise it MUST be invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: The company asks the trusted authority for a note and shows its own ID. The badge office then checks the signature, the dates, the numbers and the stamp, and says yes only if everything matches.

sections.title: Serving the Certificate to Relying Parties
sections.content:
PASSporTs are signed JSON Web Signature objects and may point to the signing certificate with an x5u header URL. That URL is expected to answer a plain GET request, while the ACME certificate URL requires POST-as-GET. So today the ACME client generally has to download the certificate and host it on a public URL.

The RFC defines an optional shortcut: when the order is ready, the ACME server can add a new x5u field to the order object, giving a URL where the CA itself hosts the certificate. Publication at that URL should follow the GET requirement and be timely with respect to the certificate life cycle.

Section 8 adds a usage note: for a complex, noncontiguous set of telephone numbers, best practice may be to split it into multiple STI certificates covering the contiguous parts, particularly if the identifier value grows too large.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of making the company put its badge on a public notice board itself, the badge office can display the badge and give out the address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The token carries the authority to represent a telephone number, a block of numbers, or a whole SPC. Creating, transporting and storing it MUST follow the strictest security best practices, beyond using encrypted transports, to keep it from anyone who would impersonate telephone numbers.

The RFC inherits the security properties of RFC 9447, and implementations should follow the best practices in RFC 8725. Only SHA256 is specified for the fingerprint hash, but the syntax would allow other algorithms if a stronger one were needed in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed note is as valuable as a key to the phone numbers, so it has to be kept very safe.

items.title: tkvalue
items.text: Required. The base64url DER-encoded TNAuthList extension.

items.title: ca
items.text: Optional. True if the certificate may be a CA certificate; false by default.

items.text: Required. Ties the token to the ACME account key.
